body.heading: Layers of ice, one trip at a time
paragraphs: A hailstone begins as a small ice pellet in a thunderstorm's powerful updraft — rising air that can exceed 100 kilometres per hour in severe storms. As the pellet is carried upward through a region of supercooled water droplets, the droplets freeze onto it, adding a layer of ice.

If the stone falls into weaker air and is caught by the updraft again, it may make several trips, gaining a new layer each time. Slice a large hailstone and you can count the journeys in its rings, alternating clear and milky ice laid down under different conditions. The stone falls for good only when its weight beats the updraft.

body.heading: From peas to grapefruits
paragraphs: Most hail is pea- to marble-sized and more nuisance than danger. But the strongest storms grow stones the size of golf balls, tennis balls, and in rare recorded cases far larger — the heaviest reliably measured hailstone, from Bangladesh, weighed about a kilogram.

Hail is a summer phenomenon precisely because it needs violent warm-season thunderstorms with towering updrafts reaching into sub-zero air. The ice at your feet on a hot afternoon fell from a part of the sky where it is always winter.

takeaway: Hail grows layer by layer inside thunderstorm updrafts until the stones are too heavy for the rising air to hold.
